package.title: On a GLP-1 Before Surgery? What a 2-Million-Record Study Found

social.instagram_caption:
On a GLP-1 with surgery coming up? A new observational study found a link, not proof.

In 2.03 million U.S. records of adults having elective surgery over 1 hour with at least 24 h in hospital (2016–2024), those on a GLP-1 medicine had lower odds of major heart complications and infections.

Matched analysis: 114,249 GLP-1 users vs 360,168 non-users, matched for age, health conditions and surgery type.
Major heart complications (heart attack, heart injury, stroke, death): GLP-1 1.0% vs no GLP-1 1.1%, 11% lower odds (relative).
Infections (wound, urinary, pneumonia, sepsis): GLP-1 4.9% vs no GLP-1 5.3%, 8% lower odds (relative).
Presented at a medical conference (Oct 2026), not yet published in a journal. Researchers say more research is needed to know if the medicines cause this.

This isn't a reason to start a GLP-1 before surgery. If you're on one, tell your surgery team and anesthesia team (and mention any nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation), and don't stop or change your medicines on your own.

Save this for your pre-op appointment, or share it with someone who has surgery coming up.

#GLP1 #SurgeryPrep #PreOpCare #MedicalResearch #AnesthesiaCare

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation — talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe to ship. I checked every number against the ASA news release and the Inside Precision Medicine report, both dated 18 Oct 2026:
- 2,028,601 patients, of whom 145,610 were GLP-1 users
- adults 18+ in the U.S., elective surgery over 60 minutes, at least 24 h in hospital, Jan 2016–Dec 2024, Epic Cosmos records
- matched groups of 114,249 users and 360,168 non-users
- major heart complications 1% vs 1.1%, adjusted OR 0.89 (11% lower odds)
- infections 4.9% vs 5.3%, adjusted OR 0.92 (8% lower odds)
- presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 meeting

The outcome definitions match the sources. The framing is right: observational, "linked to", not peer-reviewed yet, the researcher's line that more research is needed, the relative label, and absolute rates shown. MedlinePlus (revised 15 May 2026) backs the semaglutide statements: it slows stomach emptying, you should tell the doctor or dentist before surgery, and nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are common side effects. The safety lines are all there: don't stop or change your medicines on your own, this is not a reason to start a GLP-1, and the full prescriber line. Three small wording fixes would make it better. The biggest one: the source says the study didn't test whether continuing or pausing a GLP-1 right before surgery made a difference, and someone getting ready for surgery should see that.

issues.claim: Linked to lower odds, not proof, and not a reason to start a GLP-1 before surgery.
issues.problem: Inside Precision Medicine says the analysis didn't look at whether continuing or withholding a GLP-1 just before surgery affected outcomes. For a viewer with surgery coming up, leaving this out could suggest the drug is 'protective' if you keep taking it right up to surgery, which the study didn't show.
issues.fix: Slide 7 body: "Linked to lower odds, not proof, and not a reason to start a GLP-1 before surgery. The study didn't test whether continuing or pausing it before surgery made a difference. Tell your surgery team you take a GLP-1. Don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice: talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you."

issues.claim: Groups matched for similar age, health conditions and surgery type.
issues.problem: The source says the groups were matched on 'similar demographic characteristics, medical conditions and surgical procedures' and then adjusted for diabetes and prior opioid/NSAID use. 'Age' is narrower than what the source says.
issues.fix: "Groups matched for similar demographics, health conditions and surgery type, then adjusted for diabetes and past opioid or NSAID use."

issues.claim: 11% lower odds, relative / 8% lower odds, relative
issues.problem: Both figures are adjusted odds ratios (0.89 and 0.92). The estimand label 'adjusted' is missing.
issues.fix: Item 1 detail: "1.0% GLP-1 vs 1.1% no GLP-1; 11% lower adjusted odds, relative". Item 2 detail: "4.9% GLP-1 vs 5.3% no GLP-1; 8% lower adjusted odds, relative".
